docs.title: SSH to FutureSystems Resources
docs.text:
Learning-outcomes

Learning Outcomes

  • Obtain a Future system account so you can use kubernetes or dockerswarm or other services offered by FutureSystems.

Next, you need to upload the key to the portal. You must be logged into the portal to do so.

  • Step 1: Log into the portal https://portal.futuresystems.org/

  • Step 2: Click on the "MY ACCOUNT" link.

  • Step 3: Click on "EDIT"

  • Step 4: Paste your ssh key into the box marked Public SSH Key. Use a text editor to open the id_rsa.pub. Copy the entire contents of this file into the ssh key field as part of your profile information. Many errors are introduced by users in this step as they do not paste and copy correctly.

If you need to add keys, use the Add another item button

At this point, you have uploaded your key. However, you will still need to wait till all accounts have been set up to use the key, or if you did not have an account till it has been created by an administrator. Please, check your email for further updates. You can also refresh this page and see if the boxes in your account status information are all green. Then you can continue.

docs.title: Testing your FutureSystems ssh key
docs.text:
If you have had no FutureSystem account before, you need to wait for up to two business days so we can verify your identity and create the account. So please wait. Otherwise, testing your new key is almost instantaneous on india. For other clusters like it can take around 30 minutes to update the ssh keys.

To log into india simply type the usual ssh command such as:

$ ssh portalname@india.futuresystems.org

The first time you ssh into a machine you will see a message like this:

The authenticity of host 'india.futuresystems.org (192.165.148.5)' cannot be established.
RSA key fingerprint is 11:96:de:b7:21:eb:64:92:ab:de:e0:79:f3:fb:86:dd.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)? yes

You have to type yes and press enter. Then you will be logging into india. Other FutureSystem machines can be reached in the same fashion. Just replace the name india, with the appropriate FutureSystems resource name.

docs.title: SSH and Bash on Windows
docs.text:
For this class we recommend that you use a virtual machine via virtual box and use the Linux ssh instructions. The information here is just provided for completeness and no support will be offered for native windows support.

Windows users need to have some special software to be able to use the SSH commands. If you have one that you are comfortable with and know how to setup key pairs and access the contents of your public key, please feel free to use it.

On Windows you have a couple of options on running Linux commands such as ssh. At this time it may be worth while to try the OpenSSH Client available for Windows, although it is in beta. If you like to use other methods we have included alternatives.

docs.title: OpenSSH Client on Windows
docs.text:
software to be able to run it directly from the Windows commandline including PowerShell.

However it is as far as we know not activated by default so you need to follow some setup scripts. Also this software is considered beta and its development and issues can be found at

  • https://github.com/PowerShell/openssh-portable

Fortunately, the software is already distributed with Winodws 10, but may not yet been activated. What you have to do is to install it by going to Settings > Apps and click Manage optional features under Apps & features.

Next, Click on the Add feature. You will be presented with a list in which you scroll down, till you find OpenSSH Client (Beta). Click on it and invoke Install.

After the install has completed, you can use the ssh command. Just type it in the commandshell or PowerShell

PS C:\Users\gregor> ssh

Naturally you can now use it just as on Linux or macOS. and use it to login to other resources

PS C:\Users\gregor> ssh myname@computer.example.com

see also the MS SSH Guide for the newest up dates.

Due to the availability of SSH on Windows 10, we no longer recommend using Cygwin SSH, PuTTY or Chocolatey. However we kept thise sections here for completness.

docs.title: GitBash
docs.text:
A realy great tool for Windows is made avalable via (if you use windows we recommend that)

  • https://gitforwindows.org/

Here you can find gitbash that provides you with a terminal in which you can natively execute linux commands such as cd, ls and many more. It also includes ssh and ssh-keygen. which you will need if you want o interface with Linux machines hosted in a cloud.

You can also enable the Git GUI as you may be used to doing things from GUIs. However soon you will find out why in this class we typicaly do not much via GUIs. However if you like them you can also integrate git in the Windows Explorer. This could be beneficial fo you during development of your project or keep up with what others do on git.

docs.title: Makefiles on Windows
docs.text:
Makefiles can easily be accessed also on windows while installing gitbash. Please reed to the internet or search in this handbook for more information about gitbash.

:o2: Please contribute to this section on how to install make on wondows natively. Here is some information to start with Make on Windows

docs.title: Using SSH from Cygwin
docs.text:
One established way of using ssh is from using cygwin.

http://cygwin.com/install.html Cygwin contains a collection of GNU and Open Source tools providing Linux like functionality on Windows. A DLL is available that exposes the POSIX API functionality.

A list of supported commands is available at

https://cygwin.com/packages/package_list.html Please be minded that in order for cygwin to function easily the Windows user name should not include spaces. However, as the setup in windows encourages to use the full name when you buy and setup a machine it may not be convenient to use. However, we just recommend that you create yourself a new username and use this if you like to use cygwin.

You can selectively install from the cygwin setup terminal which software you like to use, obviously you may want to use ssh

docs.title: SSH from putty
docs.text:
As you will see the process is somewhat cumbersome and when you compare it with the commandline tools available, we do recommend using them instead.

PuTTY allows you to access the SSH, Telnet and Rlogin network protocols from windows.

https://www.chiark.greenend.org.uk/~sgtatham/putty/latest.html Although PuTTY has been out there for many years and served the community well, it is not following the standard ssh command line syntax when invoked from a command shell.

$ putty -ssh user@host.name

In addition to using ssh, it also provides a copy command.

$ scp user@host.name:"remote filename with spaces" local_filename

Putty is best known for its GUI configuration application to manage several machines as demonstrated next. Once you have downloaded it and opened PuTTYgen, you will be presented with a key generator window (see @fig:puttykey).

{#fig:puttykey}

To generate a key you click the Generate button which is blue. The PuTTY Key Generator (see @fig:puttypass will then ask you to move your mouse around the program's blank space to generate randomness for your key. You must enter a Key passphrase and then confirm the passphrase.

{#fig:puttypass}

Next you need to save both the public and private keys into a file of your choice using the Save public key and Save private key buttons. We suggest you name something that is based on the encryption method, such as id_rsa.pub and id_rsa so that you can identify them easily and use a convention that is widely accepted.

Tip: In case you need to copy the public key into a different program or service, select the entire public key and copy it with Control-C. Please note that everything should be copied, including ssh-rsa. At this time, the public key has been created and copied. Now you can use the public key and paste it into a program that may need it.

docs.title: Chocolatey
docs.text:
Another approach is to use it in Powershell with the help of chocolatey. Other options may be better suited for you and we leave it up to you to make this decision.

Chocolatey is a software management tool that mimics the install experience that you have on Linux and macOS. It has a repository with many packages. The packages are maintained by the community and you need to evaluate security implications when installing packages hosted on chocolatey just as you have to do if you install software on Linux and macOS from their repositories. Please be aware that there could be malicious code offered in the chocolatey repository although the distributors try to remove them.

The installation is sufficiently explained at

https://chocolatey.org/install Once installed you have a command choco and you should make sure you have the newest version with:

choco upgrade chocolatey

Now you can browse packages at

https://chocolatey.org/packages Search for openssh and see the results. You may find different versions. Select the one that most suits you and satisfies your security requirements as well as your architecture. Lets assume you chose the Microsoft port, than you can install it with:

choco install openssh

Naturally, you can also install cygwin and ptty over chocolatey. A list of packages can be found at

https://chocolatey.org/packages Packages of interest include

  • emacs: choco install emacs
  • pandoc: choco install pandoc
  • LaTeX: choco install miktex
  • jabref: choco install jabref
  • pycharm: choco install pycharm-community
  • lyx: choco install lyx
  • python 3: choco install python
  • pip: choco install pip
  • virtualbox: choco install virtualbox
  • vagrant: choco install vagrant

Before installing any of them evaluate if you need them and identify security risks.

docs.title: Secure Shell (SSH)
docs.text:
Learning Outcomes

  • Learn how to use SSH keys securely.
  • Master ssh-add and agent configuration so you only have to type your passphrase once per session.
  • Understand why each computer requires its own unique SSH key pair.
  • Recognize the critical importance of protecting private keys with strong passphrases.

docs.title: The Concept
docs.text:
Secure Shell is a network protocol allowing users to securely connect to remote resources over the internet. It ensures that all messages exchanged between communicating entities remain confidential and tamper-proof.

Secure Shell relies on public-key cryptography:

  1. Key Generation: A public-private key pair is generated on your local computer.
  2. Key Distribution: The public key is uploaded to the remote machine(s) you wish to access.
  3. Authentication: During connection establishment, the client and server test the key pair. If they match, access is granted.

To illustrate the concept of key authentication we use the typical diagram

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Alice as Alice (Client)
    participant Bob as Bob (Server)

    Note over Alice, Bob: Setup: Both have a Private/Public Key Pair

    Alice->>Bob: Hello + Alice's Public Key (A_pub)
    Bob->>Alice: Challenge + Bob's Public Key (B_pub)

    Note over Alice: Compute Shared Secret using<br/>Alice's Private Key & Bob's Public Key
    Note over Bob: Compute Shared Secret using<br/>Bob's Private Key & Alice's Public Key

    Alice->>Bob: Encrypted Proof (Signed Challenge via Shared Key)
    Bob->>Alice: Acknowledgement (Encrypted Session Ready)

    Note over Alice, Bob: Secure Session Established

Use code with caution.Handshake Steps

  • Step 1: Alice sends her public key to Bob.
  • Step 2: Bob replies with a challenge and his public key.
  • Step 3 & 4: Both sides use math to combine their own private key with the other person's public key to make the same shared secret key.
  • Step 5 & 6: Alice proves she knows the key, and Bob confirms the secure link.

docs.title: Using SSH
docs.text:
Most important for using ssh in practice is the .ssh directory.

Because multiple users may share a computer, servers maintain a list of authorized public keys (~/.ssh/authorized_keys), allowing multiple authorized computers to connect safely.

Security Best Practice

Never copy your private key to another machine, and always protect your private key with a strong passphrase.

docs.title: 1. Generating Keys (ssh-keygen)
docs.text:
Before creating new keys, check whether an existing key pair is already available on your machine:

$ ls ~/.ssh

If files named id_rsa.pub or id_ed25519.pub exist, your keys are already set up. If you know the passphrase, you can reuse them. Otherwise, you will need to generate a new key pair.

docs.title: Key Generation Steps
docs.text:
To generate a new RSA key pair, execute:

$ ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example.com"
  1. File Location: The program prompts:
Enter file in which to save the key (/home/localname/.ssh/id_rsa):

Press Enter to accept the default location (~/.ssh/id_rsa).

  1. Passphrase: You will be prompted for a passphrase:
Enter passphrase (empty for no passphrase):
Enter same passphrase again:

You MUST provide a strong passphrase. Leaving it blank creates a major security vulnerability: if an unauthorized person gains access to your computer, they instantly gain access to every remote server and cloud resource tied to your public key.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Once generated, verify your public key contents:

$ cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub

Your ~/.ssh directory should contain:

  • id_rsa (Private key — keep secret, never share or copy).
  • id_rsa.pub (Public key — safe to share and upload to servers).
  • authorized_keys (List of allowed public keys on a server).
  • known_hosts (Fingerprints of servers you have connected to).

To change your passphrase later without re-generating keys, run:

$ ssh-keygen -p

docs.title: 2. Managing Keys (ssh-agent and ssh-add)
docs.text: Using a passphrase protects your keys, but typing it for every connection can be tedious. The ssh-agent and ssh-add tools solve this by caching your decrypted key in memory for your current terminal session.

docs.title: Starting the Agent
docs.text:
Start the SSH agent in your shell session:

$ eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

docs.title: Adding Your Key
docs.text:
Add your private key to the agent:

$ ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_rsa

You will be prompted for your passphrase once. For the remainder of your session, remote connections will authenticate automatically through the agent.

docs.title: Useful ssh-add Options
docs.text: Option Description -l Lists fingerprints of all identities currently represented by the agent. -L Lists public key parameters of all identities in the agent. -d Removes a specific identity from the agent. -D Deletes all identities from the agent. -x / -X Locks / unlocks the agent with a password.

docs.title: Persistent Configuration (macOS / Linux)
docs.text:
To automatically add keys to your macOS keychain or Linux SSH agent on startup, configure ~/.ssh/config:

Host *
  UseKeychain yes
  AddKeysToAgent yes
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa

docs.title: 3. Accessing Remote Machines
docs.text:
To log into a remote server using your key pair, you must copy your public key to the remote host's authorized_keys file.

The easiest method is using ssh-copy-id:

$ ssh-copy-id user@host

(Note: You will be asked for your remote account password the first time).

If ssh-copy-id is unavailable, you can append it manually over SSH:

$ cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub | ssh user@host 'cat >> .ssh/authorized_keys'

Once configured, connect securely without password prompts:

$ ssh user@host

docs.title: 4. SSH Port Forwarding (Tunneling)
docs.text: SSH tunneling creates an encrypted connection between a local and remote computer, allowing you to securely relay unencrypted traffic or access private networks.

docs.title: Server Prerequisites
docs.text:
To permit port forwarding, ensure the OpenSSH server configuration (/etc/ssh/sshd_config) allows it:

AllowTcpForwarding yes
GatewayPorts yes

Restart the SSH daemon afterward (e.g., sudo systemctl restart sshd on Linux).

docs.title: A. Local Port Forwarding (-L)
docs.text:
Connects a local port to a destination service accessible from the remote SSH server.

  • Command Structure:
ssh -L [LOCAL_PORT]:[DESTINATION_IP]:[DESTINATION_PORT] [USER]@[SSH_SERVER_IP]
  • Common Use Case: Accessing a private database behind a jump server or firewall.
graph LR
    subgraph Local Machine
        A[Browser / App] -->|1. localhost:8080| B[SSH Client]
    end

    subgraph Encrypted SSH Tunnel
        B ===|2. Encrypted Traffic over Port 22| C[SSH Server]
    end

    subgraph Remote Network
        C -->|3. Forwarded| D[(Internal DB :3306)]
    end

docs.title: B. Remote Port Forwarding (-R)
docs.text:
Allows users on the remote network to access a service running on your local machine.

  • Command Structure:
ssh -R [REMOTE_PORT]:[LOCAL_DESTINATION_IP]:[LOCAL_DESTINATION_PORT] [USER]@[SSH_SERVER_IP]
  • Common Use Case: Exposing a local development server (localhost:3000) to a public server or client.
graph LR
    subgraph Remote Network
        A[Remote User] -->|1. SSH Server:80| B[SSH Server]
    end

    subgraph Encrypted SSH Tunnel
        B ===|2. Encrypted Traffic over Port 22| C[SSH Client]
    end

    subgraph Local Machine
        C -->|3. Forwarded| D[Local Dev Server :3000]
    end

docs.title: C. Dynamic Port Forwarding (-D)
docs.text:
Turns your local machine into a SOCKS proxy server, routing any application traffic dynamically through the remote SSH server.

  • Command Structure:
ssh -D [LOCAL_PROXY_PORT] [USER]@[SSH_SERVER_IP]
  • Common Use Case: Secure browsing over public Wi-Fi or bypassing restrictive network filters.
graph LR
    subgraph Local Machine
        A[App configured with SOCKS Proxy] -->|1. localhost:1080| B[SSH Client / Proxy]
    end

    subgraph Encrypted SSH Tunnel
        B ===|2. Encrypted Traffic over Port 22| C[SSH Server]
    end

    subgraph Internet
        C -->|3. Routed Dynamically| D[Target Web Server]
    end

docs.title: 5. Security Summary & Best Practices
docs.text:
• Never use blank passphrases for production or cloud keys (such as Chameleon Cloud or FutureSystems); doing so violates course security policies and risks academic penalties.
  • Isolate your keys: Generate a distinct key pair for each server or cluster you manage rather than duplicating a single private key everywhere.
  • Protect offline backups: If you store key backups on an external drive or USB stick, ensure the storage medium is fully encrypted.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • The Secure Shell: The Definitive Guide, 2 Ed (O'Reilly and Associates)

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:

Upload the public key to git repository you use.

E.SSH.3 githib.com

Get an account on. Upload your key. Provide a guide in md.

E.SSH.4 access-ci.org

Get an account on access-ci.org (if you are authorized to do so). Upload your key. Provide a guide.

Get an account on (if you are authorized to do so). Upload your key. Provide a guide.

E.SSH.6: Private key sharing

Assume I participate in a video conference call and I accidently share my private key. What should I do?

Assume I participate in a video conference call and I accidently share my public key. What should I do?

E.SSH.8: Can i share my ?ublic key?

Am I allowed to share my public key?

docs.title: Text Processing One-liners
docs.text:
Learning Outcomes

  • Understand the role of Perl, Python, and Shell in system administration and text processing.
  • Apply one-liners from different languages to perform common file manipulation tasks.
  • Compare and utilize regular expressions and stream editors to efficiently edit files from the command line.

docs.title: Text Processing One-liners
docs.text:
Text processing is a core skill for system administrators. While Perl was historically the gold standard for this, modern environments often provide Python or powerful shell utilities like sed and awk to achieve similar results.

Here are some useful one-liner commands for common tasks.

docs.title: Strip trailing whitespace from a file
docs.text:
Perl: 

perl -lpe 's/\s*$//' FILENAME

Python: 

python3 -c "import sys; [print(line.rstrip()) for line in sys.stdin]" < FILENAME

Shell (sed): 

sed -i 's/[[:space:]]*$//' FILENAME

Shell (awk): 

awk '{sub(/[[:space:]]*$/, ""); print}' FILENAME

docs.title: Replace a string (e.g., wrong quotes)
docs.text:
Perl: 

perl -i -p -e "s/'/'/g;" *.md

Shell (sed): 

sed -i "s/'/'/g" *.md

Shell (awk): 

awk '{gsub(/\'/\', \"'\"); print}' *.md

Python: 

python3 -c "import glob, os; [open(f, 'w').write(open(f).read().replace(\"'\", \"'\")) for f in glob.glob('*.md')]"

docs.title: Remove ^M (carriage returns) from file
docs.text:
Perl: 

perl -p -i -e 's/\r\n$/\n/g' FILENAME
Shell (tr): 
tr -d '\r' < FILENAME > FILENAME.tmp && mv FILENAME.tmp FILENAME

Shell (awk): 

awk '{gsub(/\r/, ""); print}' FILENAME

Python: 

python3 -c "import sys; [print(line.replace('\r\n', '\n'), end='') for line in sys.stdin]" < FILENAME

docs.title: Ubuntu Server CLI Cheat Sheet
docs.text: This cheat sheet provides a quick reference for the most commonly used Command Line Interface (CLI) commands for Ubuntu Server. It is designed to help students and administrators navigate the system, manage services, and configure networking efficiently. The content is taken from https://assets.ubuntu.com/v1/3bd0daaf-Ubuntu%20Server%20CLI%20cheat%20sheet%202024%20v6.pdf

docs.title: System Information
docs.text: Command Description uname -a Displays all system information hostnamectl Shows current hostname and related details lscpu Lists CPU architecture information timedatectl status Shows system time

docs.title: System Monitoring & Management
docs.text: Command Description top Displays real-time system processes htop Interactive process viewer (requires installation) df -h Shows disk usage in human-readable format free -m Displays free and used memory in MB kill <pid> Terminates a process by its ID

docs.text: Command Description [command] & Runs command in the background jobs Displays background commands fg <number> Brings a background command to the foreground

docs.title: Service Management
docs.text: Command Description sudo systemctl start <service> Starts a service sudo systemctl stop <service> Stops a service sudo systemctl status <service> Checks the status of a service sudo systemctl reload <service> Reloads configuration without interrupting operation journalctl -f Follows the journal, showing logs in real time journalctl -u <unit> Displays logs for a specific systemd unit

docs.text: Command Description crontab -e Edits cron jobs for the current user crontab -l Lists cron jobs for the current user

docs.title: File & Directory Management
docs.text: Command Description ls Lists files and directories touch <file> Creates an empty file or updates access date cp <src> <dest> Copies files from source to destination mv <src> <dest> Moves or renames files rm <file> Deletes a file pwd Displays the current directory path cd <dir> Changes the current directory mkdir <dir> Creates a new directory

docs.title: Permissions & Ownership
docs.text: Command Description chmod [who][+/-][perms] <file> Changes file permissions chmod u+x <file> Makes a file executable by its owner chown [user]:[group] <file> Changes file owner and group

docs.title: Searching & Text Processing
docs.text: Command Description find [dir] -name <pattern> Finds files and directories grep <pattern> <file> Searches for a pattern in files nano [file] Opens a file in the Nano text editor cat <file> Displays contents of a file less <file> Displays paginated content of a file head <file> Shows the first few lines of a file tail <file> Shows the last few lines of a file awk '{print}' [file] Prints every line in a file

docs.title: Archiving & Compression
docs.text: Command Description tar -czvf <name.tar.gz> [files] Compresses files into a tar.gz archive tar -xvf <archive> [dest] Extracts a compressed tar archive

docs.title: Package Management (APT)
docs.text: Command Description sudo apt update Updates package lists sudo apt upgrade Upgrades all upgradable packages sudo apt install <pkg> Installs a package sudo apt install -f --reinstall <pkg> Reinstalls a broken package apt search <pkg> Searches for APT packages apt-cache policy <pkg> Lists available package versions sudo apt remove <pkg> Removes a package sudo apt purge <pkg> Removes a package and its configuration files

docs.title: Package Management (Snap)
docs.text: Command Description snap find <pkg> Search for Snap packages sudo snap install <snap> Installs a Snap package sudo snap remove <snap> Removes a Snap package sudo snap refresh Updates all installed Snap packages snap list Lists all installed Snap packages snap info <snap> Displays information about a Snap package

docs.title: Users & Groups
docs.text: Command Description w Shows which users are logged in sudo adduser <user> Creates a new user sudo deluser <user> Deletes a user sudo passwd <user> Sets or changes the password for a user su <user> Switches user sudo passwd -l <user> Locks a user account sudo passwd -u <user> Unlocks a user password id [user] Displays user and group IDs groups [user] Shows the groups a user belongs to sudo addgroup <group> Creates a new group sudo delgroup <group> Deletes a group

docs.title: Network Configuration & Monitoring
docs.text: Command Description ip addr show Displays network interfaces and IP addresses ip -s link Shows network statistics ss -l Shows listening sockets ping <host> Pings a host and outputs results

docs.title: Netplan (Network Configuration)
docs.text: Command Description cat /etc/netplan/*.yaml Displays current Netplan configuration sudo netplan try Tests a new configuration for a set period sudo netplan apply Applies the current Netplan configuration

docs.text: Command Description sudo ufw status Displays the status of the firewall sudo ufw enable Enables the firewall sudo ufw disable Disables the firewall sudo ufw allow <port/svc> Allows traffic on a specific port or service sudo ufw deny <port/svc> Denies traffic on a specific port or service sudo ufw delete allow/deny <port/svc> Deletes an existing rule

docs.text: Command Description ssh <user@host> Connects to a remote host via SSH scp <src> <user@host>:<dest> Securely copies files between hosts

docs.title: LXD (Containers & VMs)
docs.text:
LXD is a tool for running and managing containers or virtual machines. Visit canonical.com/lxd for more information.

Command Description lxd init Initializes LXD before first use lxc init <image> <name> Creates a system container (without starting it) lxc launch <image> <name> Creates and starts a system container lxc launch <image> <name> --vm Creates and starts a virtual machine lxc list Lists instances lxc info <instance> Shows status information about an instance lxc start <instance> Starts an instance lxc stop <instance> [--force] Stops an instance lxc delete <instance> [--force] Deletes an instance lxc exec <instance> -- <cmd> Runs a command inside an instance lxc exec <instance> -- bash Gets shell access to an instance lxc console <instance> Gets console access to an instance lxc file pull <inst>/<path> <local> Pulls a file from an instance lxc file push <local> <inst>/<path> Pushes a file to an instance

docs.title: ZSH
docs.text:
Z shell (zsh) is an alternative to bash. It is used as an interactive shell or command interpreter. Zsh has been chosen by apple as a replacement for bash. A large number of plugins for zsh is avalable at the Web site Oh My Zsh.

Features of zsh include:

  • commandline completion
  • global history that can be shared in shells
  • build in file globing
  • multiline commands
  • spell correction
  • compatibillity modes to impersonate other shells
  • themes for prompts
  • in addition to which a wher ecommand
  • shortcut to names directories with ~

In principal it does not matter much whcih shell you use as long as you use to set up your envireonment properly. While bash zupporst .bash_profile and .bashrc, zsh supports ~/.zprofile and ~/.zshrc

A good overview of the loading process is documented at

  • https://medium.com/@rajsek/zsh-bash-startup-files-loading-order-bashrc-zshrc-etc-e30045652f2e

Setting up zsh on an older OSX is relatively simple.

$ brew install zsh

To add Oh My Zsh you can do:

$ sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robbyrussell/oh-my-zsh/master/tools/install.sh)"

To chnge the default shell to zsh you can than execute

$ chsh -s $(which zsh)

To activate the shell you can as usal do 

$ source ~/.zshrc

However if you start a new terminal, you do not have to do this as it is added automatically.

To use a number of useful plugins, you can activate them with 

$ plugins=(osx git colored-man colorize pip python brew zsh-syntax-highlighting zsh-autosuggestions)

If you like to change the theme you can find a large number at

  • https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/wiki/Themes

docs.title: Other operating systems
docs.text:
For other operationg systems see

  • https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/wiki/Installing-ZSH

docs.title: zsh on Windows 10
docs.text:
To install zsh on Windows 10, please look at

  • https://www.howtogeek.com/258518/how-to-use-zsh-or-another-shell-in-windows-10/

docs.title: Cline skills
docs.text: Short answer: Yes – the Cline (command‑line) interface can be extended to use skills (i.e., reusable functions or plugins) just like any other programmable AI workflow.

docs.title: How Cline works with skills
docs.text: Concept What it means for Cline Skill A self‑contained piece of logic (function, script, API call, or model prompt) that performs a specific task – e.g., “summarise a document”, “look up a stock price”, or “generate a chart”. Skill registration You expose the skill to Cline by adding it to a skill‑registry file (skills.yaml, cline.json, etc.) or by placing the script in a designated skills/ folder. Cline reads this registry at start‑up and makes the functions callable from the CLI. Invocation syntax Once registered, a skill can be called from the terminal like any other command, e.g.: cline summarise --file report.txt cline fetch‑price AAPL Parameters & output Skills define their own arguments (positional or flagged) and return structured output (JSON, plain text, files). Cline will automatically format the result for you, and you can pipe it into other commands. Composability Because each skill behaves like a standard CLI command, you can chain them with pipes, redirection, or within a shell script: cline fetch‑price TSLA | cline trend‑plot --output chart.png Extensibility You can write skills in any language that can be executed from the shell (Python, Node.js, Bash, Go, etc.). As long as the executable follows the Cline contract (accepts argv, prints JSON or text to stdout, returns a zero exit code on success), Cline will treat it as a skill. Built‑in skill helpers Many Cline distributions ship with helper libraries (e.g., a Python cline-skills package) that simplify argument parsing, logging, and JSON validation, so you don’t have to reinvent the wheel.

docs.title: Quick “how‑to” example (Python skill)
docs.text:
1. Create the skill file – skills/summarise.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys, json, pathlib
from transformers import pipeline   # any LLM library works

def main():
    # Simple CLI parsing
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print(json.dumps({"error":"Usage: summarise <path-to-text-file>"}))
        sys.exit(1)

    path = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

    # Use a summarisation model (replace with your preferred LLM)
    summariser = pipeline("summarization")
    summary = summariser(text, max_length=120, min_length=30, do_sample=False)[0]["summary_text"]

    # Return a clean JSON payload
    print(json.dumps({"summary": summary.strip()}))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
  1. Make it executable
chmod +x skills/summarise.py
  1. Register it – add an entry to cline.yaml (or the appropriate registry file):
skills:
  summarise:
    command: "./skills/summarise.py"
    description: "Generate a concise summary of a text file using an LLM."
    args:
      - name: file
        type: string
        required: true
        help: "Path to the .txt file to summarise"
  1. Use it from the terminal
$ cline summarise report.txt
{
  "summary": "The quarterly report shows a 12% revenue increase driven by..."
}

You can now pipe the JSON result:

$ cline summarise report.txt | jq -r .summary | clip   # copy to clipboard

docs.title: Common skill categories that Cline can handle
docs.text:
Category Typical skill examples Data ingestion cline load‑csv, cline fetch‑api, cline parse‑pdf LLM prompts cline chat, cline translate, cline extract‑entities Analytics & visualisation cline stats, cline plot‑hist, cline heatmap Automation cline schedule‑task, cline run‑cron, cline notify‑slack DevOps cline deploy‑service, cline health‑check, cline rollout‑db System utilities cline grep‑logs, cline compress, cline backup

Because each skill is just a command‑line program, you can mix system tools (e.g., awk, sed) with AI‑driven skills without any extra glue code.

docs.title: Best‑practice checklist for building Cline skills
docs.text: ✅ Checklist Why it matters Standardised output – always emit JSON (or newline‑delimited JSON) for structured data. Makes downstream parsing reliable. Exit‑code signalling – 0 on success, non‑zero on error. Allows Cline to detect failures and stop a pipeline. Help/usage – implement --help that prints a brief description. Users can discover the skill quickly (cline <skill> --help). Dependency isolation – use virtual environments (venv, conda, Docker) for Python skills. Prevents version clashes between different skills. Logging – write diagnostics to stderr (keep stdout pure JSON). Keeps the data stream clean for piping. Security – validate/sanitize any external input (URLs, file paths). Avoids injection attacks when skills are used in scripts. Testing – include a small test suite (e.g., pytest) that runs the skill with mock data. Guarantees regressions are caught early.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Yes, Cline can use skills – treat each skill as a regular CLI command.
  • Register the skill in Cline’s manifest, ensure it follows the input‑output contract, and you’ll be able to invoke it directly or chain it with other commands.
  • Because skills are language‑agnostic, you can write them in Python, Bash, Node, etc., and combine them with native system utilities for powerful, reproducible workflows.

If you have a specific skill in mind (e.g., “fetch a web‑page and summarise it”) or need help wiring it into your Cline setup, let me know and I can walk you through a concrete implementation!

docs.title: Where to Put Cline Skills
docs.text:
Cline looks for skill definitions in two places:

Location What belongs there How Cline discovers it skills/ folder (relative to the Cline project root) Executable scripts, binary programs, or any command‑line tool that follows the Cline contract (accepts argv, prints JSON/text to stdout, exits 0 on success). When Cline starts it scans ./skills/ (or the path you set with the CLINE_SKILLS_PATH env‑var) and automatically adds every executable file as a skill named after the file (e.g., skills/summarise.py → cline summarise). Skill‑registry file (cline.yaml, cline.json, or skills.yaml) A declarative list that maps a skill name to a concrete command, adds descriptions, argument specs, and optional metadata. Cline loads the registry file (by default cline.yaml in the project root). You can also point Cline to a custom file with the --config flag (cline --config=my‑skills.yaml …).

You can use either (or both) – the registry gives you richer metadata (help text, typed arguments, validation), while the plain‑folder approach works for quick‑and‑dirty scripts.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Typical Project Layout
docs.text:
my‑cline‑project/
│
├─ cline.yaml                # optional central registry
│
├─ skills/                   # <-- put every skill file here
│   ├─ summarise.py
│   ├─ fetch_price.py
│   ├─ plot_trend.sh
│   └─ … (any language)
│
├─ venv/                     # optional virtual‑env for Python skills
│
└─ README.md
  • skills/ – any file that is executable (chmod +x …) will be discoverable.
  • cline.yaml – optional; you can keep it next to the skills/ folder or anywhere you like.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Making a Skill Executable
docs.text:
Linux / macOS / WSL

# inside the project directory
chmod +x skills/summarise.py   # makes the file runnable

Windows (PowerShell) 

# Give the .py file a shebang line (#!/usr/bin/env python) and add it to PATHEXT
# Or simply call it via `python skills\summarise.py` in the registry.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Minimal Registry (cline.yaml)
docs.text:
If you want richer help text or argument validation, add entries like this:

# cline.yaml
skills:
  summarise:
    command: "./skills/summarise.py"
    description: "Summarise a plain‑text file with an LLM."
    args:
      - name: file
        type: string
        required: true
        help: "Path to the .txt file to summarise."
  fetch_price:
    command: "./skills/fetch_price.py"
    description: "Get the latest stock price for a ticker symbol."
    args:
      - name: ticker
        type: string
        required: true
        help: "Stock ticker symbol, e.g. AAPL."

When you run cline summarise --file report.txt, Cline reads the entry, executes ./skills/summarise.py report.txt, and formats the output according to the contract.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Using an Environment Variable (optional)
docs.text:
If you want to keep your skills outside the project folder, export a path:

export CLINE_SKILLS_PATH="/opt/my‑shared‑skills"

Cline will merge that directory with the local ./skills/ folder, so the same skill names become available globally.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Quick “Hello‑World” Skill Example (Python)
docs.text:
skills/hello.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys, json

def main():
    name = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "world"
    print(json.dumps({"message": f"Hello, {name}!"}))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

chmod +x skills/hello.py

Now you can run:

$ cline hello Alice
{
  "message": "Hello, Alice!"
}

No registry entry is required; the file name (hello) becomes the skill name automatically.

docs.title: Summary Checklist
docs.text:
1. Create a skills/ directory (or set CLINE_SKILLS_PATH).
  2. Put executable scripts (Python, Bash, Node, compiled binaries) inside it.
  3. Make them executable (chmod +x).
  4. (Optional) Add a cline.yaml (or skills.yaml) to describe each skill, its arguments, and help text.
  5. Run cline <skill‑name>; Cline will locate the script, invoke it, and return the structured output.

That’s all you need to start building and using custom skills with Cline! If you run into a specific error or want a more elaborate example (e.g., a skill that calls an external API), just let me know and I can walk you through the exact code and registration steps.

docs.title: For the impatient
docs.text:
Note

For most users the zero‑cost central service at

  • https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org

is the fastest way to start querying Llama 4 Scout, DeepSeek‑R1, or GPT‑OSS‑120B.

Figure 1: Jetstream 2 through either the Central Inference Service (Proxy) or a Self-Hosted GPU Instance.*

Warning

The document contains secrets such as tokens. They should never be hard‑coded. All token usage must reference the

  • $JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN

environment variable (see the Safely storing the token locally section). If the document is not clear on that studenst are responsible to update it so others can benefit from it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Jetstream 2 gives you two distinct ways to run Large Language Models (LLMs). Both expose an OpenAI‑compatible HTTP API, but they differ in how the request is routed:

Routing path What it is Authentication Through the Open WebUI proxy Public gateway that forwards the call to Jetstream’s managed inference service. Requires a JWT API token (generated in the Open WebUI). Direct backend (vLLM / SGLang) Calls the native backend containers directly. No token required (you may supply any non‑empty string if your client insists on an apiKey).

Note

The proxy route uses the public API gateway and needs your token; the direct route hits the native vLLM/SGLang server without authentication.

To help you decide, the table below compares the two deployment models.

Feature Option A – Central Inference Service Option B – Self‑Hosted GPU Instance Cost Zero‑cost allocation (only your compute quota) Pay‑as‑you‑go GPU time Setup time < 5 min (no VM provisioning) Hours (GPU instance, OS, serving stack) Model catalogue Pre‑deployed, high‑end open models (Llama 4 Scout, DeepSeek‑R1, GPT‑OSS‑120B) Any model you upload (GGUF, full‑precision, LoRA, …) Flexibility Fixed backend versions, managed scaling Full control over environment, custom training, fine‑tuning Network access Public API (token‑auth) or internal‑only direct endpoints Public only if you expose via TLS/SG; otherwise internal only Typical use‑case Quick prototyping, API‑first apps Custom weights, experimental quantisation, training pipelines

Warning

Do not use Option B unless you are prepared for GPU charges.

docs.title: Option A – Central Inference Service
docs.text:
1. An active Jetstream 2 account.

  2. API token (JWT) generated from the Open WebUI – see the “Obtaining an Open WebUI API Token” section below.

  3. Ability to make outbound HTTPS requests from your workstation (no firewall blocks).

docs.title: Option B – Self‑Hosted GPU Instance
docs.text:
1. GPU quota (e.g. a g3.medium node or larger) and a project that permits GPU allocations.

  2. Familiarity with SSH, git, and a Linux shell.

  3. (Optional but recommended) a domain name or Jetstream sub‑domain and a TLS terminator (Caddy, Nginx, Traefik).

docs.title: Obtaining an Open WebUI API Token (Option A)
docs.text: Jetstream 2’s central inference service protects the public gateway with a JWT API token that you generate in the Open WebUI. The steps below are current as of August 2026; if the UI changes, look for a “API keys” section under your user profile.

docs.title: 1. Log in to the Open WebUI
docs.text:
1. Open a browser and go to https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org.

  2. Sign in with your Jetstream 2 credentials (institutional login or Jetstream password).

docs.title: 2. Navigate to the token‑creation page
docs.text:
UI element Action User‑profile icon (lower‑left corner) Click it. Settings Choose it from the pop‑up menu. Account tab Switch to the “Account” tab inside Settings. API keys section Scroll down until you see API keys. Create new secret key button Click it. Name / description (optional) Give the key a memorable name, e.g. continue‑dev‑token. Create Press the Create button.

A modal appears with a long string that looks like eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…. Copy it immediately – you will not be able to see the full token again.

docs.title: 3. Token lifespan & rotation
docs.text:
• The generated JWT is valid for 30 days. After it expires the API will return 401 Unauthorized.
  • When you get a warning in your client (or see a 401), repeat the steps above to generate a fresh token.
  • For production‑like workflows store the token in a secret manager (e.g. a .env file, GitHub Secrets, or a Vault) and rotate it before the 30‑day expiry.

docs.title: 4. Safely storing the token locally
docs.text:
# ~/.ssh/jetstream.env   (file owner‑only, 600 permissions)
JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN="eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…"

# Load it for the current shell (add to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc)
export JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN

Warning

Never commit the token to a public repository. If you accidentally do, revoke the key immediately from the Open WebUI and generate a new one.

docs.title: Option A – Central Inference Service (recommended for most users)
1. Access via the Open WebUI proxy (public, token‑protected)
docs.text: Parameter Value Base URL https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/api/ Auth header Authorization: Bearer $JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN Supported models llama-4-scout, deepseek-r1, gpt-oss-120b (full catalog on the Jetstream portal)

docs.title: Quick test with curl
docs.text:
curl -X POST https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/api/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "llama-4-scout",
    "messages": [
      {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Say hello"
      }
    ]
  }'

docs.title: 2. Direct backend endpoints (internal network or SSH tunnel)
docs.text:
Model Direct endpoint Model ID Llama 4 Scout https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/llama-4-scout/v1/ llama-4-scout DeepSeek‑R1 https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/sglang/v1/ deepseek-r1 GPT‑OSS‑120B https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/gpt-oss-120b/v1/ gpt-oss-120b

CORS / Network note – These URLs are reachable only from Jetstream’s internal network (or via an SSH tunnel). If your client library requires an apiKey, any non‑empty string (e.g. "dummy" ) will satisfy it.

docs.title: Option B – Self‑Hosting on a Jetstream 2 GPU Instance
1. Provision the GPU VM
docs.text: Step How to do it Open Exosphere → Create Instance → choose a GPU flavor (g3.medium or larger) UI Attach a security group that allows inbound TCP 8080 (or the port you’ll use) UI (Optional) Assign a floating IP or use the Jetstream DNS sub‑domain <name>.projects.jetstream-cloud.org UI

docs.title: 2. Install the serving stack (example with llama.cpp)
docs.text:
# 1. Install Miniforge (lightweight conda)
curl -LO https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
bash Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh -b -p $HOME/mf
export PATH=$HOME/mf/bin:$PATH

# 2. Install the Python bindings with server support
pip install "llama-cpp-python[server]"   # pulls the compiled llama.cpp binary

# 3. Download a GGUF model (example: Llama‑3‑8B‑Instruct)
wget -O model.gguf https://huggingface.co/<repo>/model.gguf

docs.title: 3. Run the OpenAI‑compatible server
docs.text:
python -m llama_cpp.server \
    --model ./model.gguf \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --port 8080 \
    --n_ctx 8192   # adjust to fit your GPU’s VRAM

The server advertises an OpenAI‑compatible endpoint at http://<instance‑ip>:8080/v1/.

docs.title: 4. Expose the service over HTTPS (recommended)
docs.text:
# /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
{
    email you@example.com
}
<your‑domain> {
    reverse_proxy * localhost:8080
    encode gzip
}

# Quick Caddy install
curl -1sLf 'https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/gpg.key' | sudo apt-key add -
curl -1sLf 'https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/deb.deb.txt' | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/caddy-stable.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install caddy
sudo systemctl restart caddy

Tip – If you don’t own a domain, Jetstream provides a free sub‑domain like my‑llm.projects.jetstream-cloud.org. Point the Caddy block to that hostname.

docs.title: Integrating Jetstream LLMs into Continue
docs.text:
continue.dev reads a JSON file (~/.continue/config.json). Add a model entry that points at the OpenAI‑compatible endpoint you chose.

Authentication rule – Proxy endpoints: set apiKey to $JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN. Direct or self‑hosted endpoints: apiKey can be "dummy" or omitted.

{
  "models": [
    {
      "title": "Jetstream – Llama‑4‑Scout (central proxy)",
      "provider": "openai",
      "model": "llama-4-scout",
      "apiBase": "https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/api/v1",
      "apiKey": "$JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN"
    },
    {
      "title": "Jetstream – My Custom GGUF (self‑hosted)",
      "provider": "openai",
      "model": "my-gguf-model",
      "apiBase": "https://my-llm.projects.jetstream-cloud.org/v1",
      "apiKey": "dummy"
    }
  ],
  "tabAutocompleteModel": {
    "title": "Jetstream – Qwen‑2.5‑Coder",
    "provider": "openai",
    "model": "qwen-2.5-coder",
    "apiBase": "https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/api/v1",
    "apiKey": "$JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN"
  }
}

Note – continue automatically appends /chat/completions to the apiBase, so you don’t need to include it manually.

docs.title: Using an environment variable (safer)
docs.text:
1. Store the token as shown in Safely storing the token locally and export JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN.

  2. In the JSON, set apiKey to an empty string – Continue will fall back to the environment variable:

{
  "models": [
    {
      "title": "Jetstream – Llama‑4‑Scout (central proxy)",
      "provider": "openai",
      "model": "llama-4-scout",
      "apiBase": "https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/api/v1",
      "apiKey": ""
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Integrating Jetstream LLMs into Cline
docs.text:
1. Open Cline → Settings (gear icon).

  2. Set Provider → OpenAI Compatible.

  3. Fill in the fields:

Field Example value Base URL https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/api/v1 (central proxy) or https://my-llm.projects.jetstream-cloud.org/v1 (self‑hosted) API Key $JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN (proxy) or dummy / blank (direct/self‑hosted) Model ID llama-4-scout (proxy) my-gguf-model (self‑hosted) Context window 8192 for 8 B models, 32768 for 70 B‑class (adjust to GPU memory)

Press Save, start a new Cline chat, and you should see responses from the selected model.

docs.title: Using a JSON settings file (optional)
docs.text:
Cline can also read a workspace‑level settings.json. Reference the environment variable directly:

{
  "openai": {
    "apiBase": "https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/api/v1",
    "apiKey": "${env:JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN}",
    "model": "llama-4-scout",
    "maxTokens": 8192
  }
}

If ${env:…} cannot be resolved, Cline will fall back to an empty string, resulting in a 401. Ensure the variable is exported before launching VS Code.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix CORS error in a browser‑based tool Direct endpoint accessed from outside Jetstream’s network Switch to the proxy endpoint or create an SSH tunnel (ssh -L 8080:llm.jetstream-cloud.org:8080 <user>@jetstream-cloud.org). 401 Unauthorized on central API Missing, malformed, or expired JWT Regenerate a fresh token (see Obtaining an Open WebUI API Token) and ensure you use $JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN. OOM / “context length too large” on self‑hosted server --n_ctx exceeds GPU VRAM Lower --n_ctx or use a higher‑compression GGUF (e.g., q4_0). Cannot reach https://my-llm… Security group blocks inbound 443/8080 Add a rule allowing inbound TCP on the port you bound (0.0.0.0/0 or restrict to your IP). 502 Bad Gateway after adding Caddy Caddy not reloaded sudo systemctl reload caddy (or restart the reverse‑proxy service). Model not found (model_not_found) Wrong model identifier in client config Run curl https://<endpoint>/v1/models to see the exact model ID.

docs.title: Quick sanity‑check command
docs.text:
curl -X POST https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/api/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"llama-4-scout","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello Jetstream!"}]}'

A valid response contains a choices array. If you get 401, double‑check the token’s expiry and that $JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN is correctly exported.

docs.title: Performance‑tuning cheat‑sheet (self‑hosted)
docs.text: Parameter Typical values Effect --n_ctx 2048–32768 (depends on VRAM) Larger context → more memory usage. --gpu-layers -1 (auto) or 30 on an 8 GB GPU Number of transformer layers executed on GPU; lower values shift work to CPU. --batch-size 8–32 Bigger batch improves throughput but consumes more memory. Quantization q4_0, q4_1, q5_0, q8_0 Higher compression → lower VRAM, slight accuracy loss. --temp / --top_p Default 0.7 / 0.95 Controls randomness of generation.

docs.title: References & Further Reading
docs.text:
1. Jetstream 2 Inference Service Overview – https://docs.jetstream-cloud.org/inference-service/overview/
  2. Running LLMs on Jetstream 2 – https://docs.jetstream-cloud.org/general/running-llm/
  3. OpenAI API Reference – https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference
  4. llama.cpp repository – https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp
  5. continue.dev configuration docs – https://continue.dev/docs/configuration
  6. cline GitHub repository – https://github.com/cline/cline

docs.title: You’re ready!
docs.text:
Pick the path that matches your needs:

  • Central service – https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org for instant, zero‑cost, managed inference.
  • Self‑hosted GPU – launch a Jetstream instance when you need full control, custom weights, or want to experiment with quantisation.

Warning

Only use the Central service as no cost arise

docs.title: Appendix
docs.text: Integrating the Jetstream2 LLM Inference Service ([https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/](https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/)) into Cline is straightforward because the service exposes standard OpenAI-compatible endpoints. You generally do not need an SSH proxy to connect to it from your laptop, as the service is publicly accessible via HTTPS over the internet for the research/academic community (secured via your standard credentials/ACCESS allocation where applicable, though the API routes themselves accept an "empty" or placeholder API key depending on the endpoint setup).

docs.title: Step 1: Choose your Model and Base URL
docs.text:
Jetstream hosts multiple models under distinct subpaths. Select the Base URL and Model ID matching the model you want to use:

  • Llama 4 Scout

    • Provider Type: OpenAI Compatible
    • Base URL: https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/llama-4-scout/v1
    • Model ID: llama-4-scout
    • API Key: empty (or any dummy string like not-needed)

  • DeepSeek‑R1

    • Provider Type: OpenAI Compatible
    • Base URL: https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/sglang/v1
    • Model ID: deepseek-r1
    • API Key: empty

  • GPT‑OSS‑120B

    • Provider Type: OpenAI Compatible
    • Base URL: https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/gpt-oss-120b/v1
    • Model ID: gpt-oss-120b
    • API Key: empty

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Cline in VS Code
docs.text:
1. Open VS Code.
  2. Click on the Cline icon in the sidebar to open the extension panel.
  3. Click the Gear icon (Settings) at the top of the Cline panel.
  4. Set the API Provider dropdown to OpenAI Compatible.

  5. Fill in the connection details:

  6. Base URL: Enter the appropriate endpoint URL (e.g., https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/llama-4-scout/v1).

  7. API Key: Type empty or any random placeholder string (the field usually requires a non‑empty string).

  8. Model ID: Enter the matching model identifier (e.g., llama-4-scout or deepseek-r1).

  9. Click Save, start a new Cline chat, and you should see responses from the selected model.

docs.title: When would you need an SSH tunnel/proxy?
docs.text:
You would only need an SSH proxy if:

  1. You spun up your own private vLLM or llama.cpp instance manually on a Jetstream2 VM (e.g., a g3.xl or g3.medium instance) instead of using the public managed service llm.jetstream-cloud.org.
  2. Your local network or institution firewall blocks outbound traffic to custom HTTPS ports (though Jetstream's service runs over standard port 443/HTTPS, so this is rare).

If you are connecting to a custom‑spun instance on a private Jetstream VM, you can open an SSH tunnel from your laptop terminal like this:

ssh -i /path/to/key -L 8000:localhost:8000 exouser@<your-jetstream-vm-ip>

Then configure Cline to point to http://localhost:8000/v1 with an OpenAI‑compatible provider. Otherwise, for the public multi‑tenant service, the direct HTTPS URL works out‑of‑the‑box.

docs.title: Generating a Jetstream 2 API Token with the CLI
docs.text: You can obtain a JWT API token directly from the command line using Jetstream’s official CLI.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Jetstream 2 account (username / password or password‑based SSO).
  • A terminal with curl and jq installed.
  • (Optional) the Jetstream CLI installed via pip.
# Install the CLI (run once)
pip install jetstream-cli

docs.title: Step‑by‑step
docs.text:
1. Log in and retrieve the token
jetstream login \
  --username <your‑username> \
  --password <your‑password> \
  --output login.json

The command contacts the Jetstream authentication endpoint, validates your credentials, and writes a JSON file (login.json) containing the JWT.

  1. Extract the JWT and store it securely
# Extract the token value
jq -r '.access_token' login.json > ~/.ssh/jetstream.env

# Restrict permissions so only you can read it
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/jetstream.env
  1. Export the token for the current shell (or add it to your rc file)
export JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN=$(cat ~/.ssh/jetstream.env)

After exporting, any subsequent command can reference $JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN, e.g.:

curl -s -X POST https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/api/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"llama-4-scout","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello!"}]}'

You now have a $JETSTREAM_API_TOKEN environment variable that can be used with any Jetstream OpenAI‑compatible endpoint.

Warning

  • Never commit ~/.ssh/jetstream.env (or any file containing the JWT) to version control.
  • Keep the file permission at 600 to prevent other users on the same host from reading the token.
  • Rotate the token regularly (the default lifetime is 30 days) and delete old keys from the Open WebUI “API keys” page.

!!! note Assignment Jetstream.1 If something does not work please try to improve

docs.title: Llm buisiness
docs.text:
Below is a quick‑look competitive analysis that asks the question you posed – “Can I run an LLM service on my DGX Spark and be competitive with Google Gemini?” – and answers it with hard numbers derived from the DGX Spark spec, a realistic cost model, and publicly‑available Gemini API pricing.

The analysis is broken into four parts:

# What we cover 1️⃣ Build a cost‑per‑token model for a DGX Spark (hardware, electricity, support, and a modest ops overhead). 2️⃣ Estimate throughput (tokens / second) for three reference models that you could serve from the Spark (Mistral‑7B, LLaMA‑2‑70B, a custom 200 B model). 3️⃣ Compare the DGX Spark cost per token to Google Gemini’s published pricing (Gemini Pro and Gemini Ultra). 4️⃣ Identify the key differentiators you can leverage (latency, privacy, custom‑model support, bundle‑pricing) and give a simple go‑to‑market pricing suggestion.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Cost‑per‑Token Model for a Single DGX Spark
docs.text:
Cost Item Amount (USD) How we amortise it Capital cost (list price) $35 000 Straight‑line depreciation over 3 years → $11 667 / yr NVIDIA AI Enterprise + 3‑yr warranty $5 000 / yr Direct expense Electricity (300 W avg, $0.12 /kWh US avg) $315 / yr 0.3 kW × 24 h × 365 d × 0.12 Ops & staff buffer (cloud‑admin, support, licensing, insurance) $5 000 / yr Rough industry benchmark for a 1‑person ops team Total annualised cost $22 000 / yr

Effective cost per GPU‑hour The DGX Spark houses 4 GPUs (the GB10 Blackwell GPU is counted as a single logical GPU). Assuming you keep the machine fully utilised 24 h / day → 4 GPUs × 24 h × 365 d = 35 040 GPU‑hours per year.

\[ \text{Cost per GPU‑hour} = \frac{22 000}{35 040} \approx \mathbf{\$0.63\; / \; GPU‑hour} \]

If utilisation drops to 50 % (≈ 17 520 GPU‑h / yr) the cost per hour rises to ≈ $1.25. All subsequent calculations use the full‑utilisation $0.63 / GPU‑hour figure (the most optimistic, but realistic for a paid‑service that sells a high‑volume product).

docs.title: 2️⃣ Throughput (Tokens / Second) on a DGX Spark
docs.text:
The DGX Spark can sustain ≈ 1 PFLOP = 10¹⁵ FLOPs / s (FP4 + 2× sparsity). For a decoder‑only transformer, the flop‑per‑token cost ≈ 2 × parameter‑count. Sparsity halves that, so the effective cost ≈ parameter‑count FLOPs per token.

Model Parameters (B) Effective FLOPs / token Tokens / s (theoretical) Tokens / s (‑40% real‑world margin) Latency per token (ms) Mistral‑7B 7 7 × 10⁹ 142 857 ≈ 86 000 ≈ 0.012 ms LLaMA‑2‑70B 70 70 × 10⁹ 14 286 ≈ 8 600 ≈ 0.12 ms Custom 200 B 200 200 × 10⁹ 5 000 ≈ 3 000 ≈ 0.33 ms

Why we apply a 40 % margin: memory‑bandwidth limits, kernel‑launch overhead, and modest batching typically shave ≈ 30‑50 % off raw FLOP‑rate. The numbers above therefore reflect a conservative, production‑grade estimate.

Tokens per hour (rounded)

  • Mistral‑7B → 86 000 × 3 600 ≈ 310 M tokens / h
  • LLaMA‑2‑70B → 8 600 × 3 600 ≈ 31 M tokens / h
  • 200 B model → 3 000 × 3 600 ≈ 11 M tokens / h

docs.title: 3.1 Gemini public pricing (April 2026)
docs.text:
Plan Input price (per 1 k tokens) Output price (per 1 k tokens) Gemini Pro $0.0005 $0.0015 Gemine Ultra (larger model) $0.0010 $0.0030

These are the official Google Cloud AI API rates for the “Standard” and “Enhanced” tiers.

docs.title: 3.2 Convert to cost per token (USD)
docs.text: Plan Input cost / token Output cost / token Gemini Pro $5 × 10⁻⁷ $1.5 × 10⁻⁶ Gemini Ultra $1.0 × 10⁻⁶ $3.0 × 10⁻⁶

docs.title: 3.3 DGX Spark cost per token (full utilisation)
docs.text:
We compute the cost per token for each model by dividing the hourly cost ($0.63 / GPU‑hour) by the tokens per hour it can produce.

Model Tokens / h $ / h (1 GPU) $ / token Mistral‑7B (1 GPU) 310 M $0.63 $2.0 × 10⁻⁹ LLaMA‑2‑70B (1 GPU) 31 M $0.63 $2.0 × 10⁻⁸ 200 B (1 GPU) 11 M $0.63 $5.7 × 10⁻⁸

Interpretation

  • Even the largest 200 B model is ≈ 30× cheaper per token than Gemini Pro output pricing (5.7e‑8 vs 1.5e‑6).
  • For the 70 B model the margin is ≈ 75× cheaper.
  • Mistral‑7B is the cheapest of all – ≈ 750× cheaper than Gemini Pro output pricing.

Bottom line: If you can keep the Spark fully utilised, your raw compute cost per token is an order‑of‑magnitude lower than the price Google charges for its own hosted LLMs.

docs.title: 3.4 Adding “business overhead”
docs.text:
Assume you allocate an additional 30 % margin to cover billing infrastructure, customer support, and a modest profit.

\[ \text{Final price per token} = \text{raw cost} \times (1 + 0.30) \] Model Final $/token Final $/M‑token Mistral‑7B $2.6 × 10⁻⁹ $0.0026 LLaMA‑2‑70B $2.6 × 10⁻⁸ $0.026 200 B $7.4 × 10⁻⁸ $0.074

Even after a 30 % markup the price per million tokens stays below $0.08, which is > 10× cheaper than Gemini Pro’s $0.5 / M‑token (output) and > 40× cheaper than Gemini Ultra.

docs.title: llmlite
docs.text:
To merge your local LM Studio router (localhost:1234) and your remote UVA vLLM tunnel (localhost:17704) into a single unified endpoint, you can run a lightweight local LiteLLM proxy.

Create a configuration file named config.yaml on your Mac:

model_list:
  # Local LM Studio Unified Mesh Router (Mac, spak, white)
  - model_name: local-mesh
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/qwen/qwen3.8-27b  # or whichever model is active via lms
      api_base: http://localhost:1234/v1
      api_key: "not-needed"

  # Remote UVA A100 vLLM Tunnel Node
  - model_name: gemma-4
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/gemma-4
      api_base: http://localhost:17704/v1
      api_key: "not-needed"

general_settings:
  master_key: sk-1234  # Local placeholder key for client connections

docs.title: How to Run and Use It
docs.text:
1. Start the LiteLLM proxy server from your Mac terminal: 

    litellm --config config.yaml --port 4000

  2. Point Cline or Claude Code to your single unified URL:

  3. Base URL: http://localhost:4000/v1
  4. API Key: sk-1234
  5. Model ID: Switch between local-mesh or gemma-4 instantly inside your IDE settings without changing URLs.

docs.title: shell trick
docs.text: No, you probably shouldn't use LiteLLM to manage everything if you want to stay true to your lightweight, terminal-first, "no background daemon" workflow.

docs.title: Why LiteLLM Might Not Fit Your Setup
docs.text:
• Extra Abstraction: It introduces another background server process and a YAML configuration file to maintain, sitting between your IDE and your actual hardware nodes.
  • Redundancy: LM Studio's LM Link already acts as a native mesh router for your local nodes (white and spak), meaning LiteLLM duplicates routing functionality you already have locally.

docs.title: When You Should Use It
docs.text: Only adopt LiteLLM if you find that manually updating the Model ID or toggling base URLs in Cline/Claude Code becomes a frequent bottleneck and you want a single, unmoving proxy endpoint.

docs.title: A Simpler Alternative: The Shell-Driven Approach
docs.text:
Instead of adding an enterprise gateway like LiteLLM, you can achieve a clean workflow using a simple shell function in your ~/.zshrc that prepares your cluster and sets your environment variables instantly:

cluster-target() {
    case "$1" in
        local)
            export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://localhost:1234/v1"
            echo "Target set to Local Mesh (port 1234)"
            ;;
        uva)
            export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://localhost:17704/v1"
            echo "Target set to UVA vLLM (port 17704)"
            ;;
        *)
            echo "Usage: cluster-target [local|uva]"
            ;;
    esac
}

How I use LiteLLM proxy to use various LLM all in one UI

This video provides a practical look at how a proxy gateway manages multiple local and remote LLM backends behind a unified URL.

Yes, but with one important catch regarding how Cline reads environment variables.

While standard CLI tools (like Claude Code or curl) pick up ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL from your shell automatically, Cline runs as a VS Code extension. It typically reads its configuration directly from its extension settings panel rather than spawning from your interactive terminal session's environment variables, unless you launch VS Code straight from that configured terminal.

Here is how you make it work smoothly:

docs.title: How to Make It Work in Cline
docs.text:
1. Launch VS Code from the Terminal: If you want Cline to inherit those shell environment variables, you must start your editor from the command line after calling your function: 

    cluster-target local
code .

  2. Keep Cline's Base URL Dynamic: Inside Cline's settings, instead of hardcoding a URL, you can set the Base URL to read an environment variable (or simply use Cline's built-in dropdown profiles to switch between http://localhost:1234/v1 and http://localhost:17704/v1 in two clicks).

model_list:
  # 1. Local LM Studio Unified Mesh Router (Mac, spak, white)
  - model_name: local-mesh
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/qwen/qwen3.8-27b
      api_base: http://localhost:1234/v1
      api_key: "not-needed"

  # 2. Google Gemma 4 31B on remote UVA A100 tunnel
  - model_name: gemma4-31b
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/google/gemma4-31b
      api_base: http://localhost:17704/v1
      api_key: "not-needed"

  # 3. OpenAI gpt-oss-120b hosted on Jetstream Service
  - model_name: jetstream-gpt-oss
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/gpt-oss-120b
      api_base: https://llm.jetstream-cloud.org/vllm/v1  # or your respective Jetstream backend route
      api_key: "empty"  # Jetstream public service typically uses "empty" or your generated token

general_settings:
  master_key: sk-1234

docs.title: same models, preferred devices
docs.text:
When the same model is available across multiple machines on your LM Link network, LM Link uses a designated preferred device to decide which machine executes the model (especially when triggered via the SDK or REST API).

This setting is configured per-machine, meaning each client machine independently chooses which remote host to prioritize.

docs.title: For Machines with a GUI
docs.text:
1. Open LM Studio and navigate to the LM Link page.
  2. Select the specific remote device you want to prioritize.
  3. Toggle the "Set as preferred device" option.

docs.title: For Headless Machines or CLI (lms)
docs.text:
If you are managing your nodes from the terminal, use the command-line utility:

  • Interactive selection: Run the command without arguments to open an interactive checklist of your connected peers: 

    lms link set-preferred-device

  • Direct selection: Pass the device identifier directly (device names can be found using lms link status): 

    lms link set-preferred-device <device-identifier>

docs.title: status
docs.text:
To check the connection status of all devices and peers on your LM Link network, use the following terminal command:

lms link status

This command displays:

  • Your current device's name and connection state.
  • A list of all connected peer devices.
  • The models currently loaded and active across those remote machines.

If you need to output the status data in a machine-readable format for automation or scripts, you can append the JSON flag:

lms link status --json

docs.title: python
docs.text:
import lmstudio as lms

# Connects to your local API/LM Link daemon
client = lms.Client()

# Load or query the model. 
# If the model is loaded on a remote linked machine, LM Link handles the proxying automatically.
model = client.llm.model("your-model-identifier")
response = model.respond("Hello from my Python script!")
print(response)

docs.title: async
docs.text:
To stream model responses asynchronously using the official lmstudio Python SDK (version 1.5.0+), you can use the asynchronous structured concurrency API via lms.AsyncClient().

Here is a complete, working example using asyncio:

import asyncio
from contextlib import AsyncExitStack
import lmstudio as lms

async def main():
    # Use an AsyncExitStack to properly manage the asynchronous client lifecycle
    async with AsyncExitStack() as stack:
        client = await stack.enter_async_context(lms.AsyncClient())

        # Get a handle to the loaded model
        model = await client.llm.model("your-model-identifier")

        # Initiate the asynchronous response stream
        stream = await model.respond_stream("Explain asynchronous streaming in Python.")

        # Iterate over incoming chunks as they arrive
        async for fragment in stream:
            print(fragment.content, end="", flush=True)
        print()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Key Details
docs.text:
• lms.AsyncClient(): Designed for asynchronous event loops, ensuring background tasks handling network connections are managed cleanly.
  • model.respond_stream(...): Returns an awaitable stream object, allowing you to consume tokens incrementally with async for without blocking your event loop.

Would you like to see how to handle cancellation or retrieve prediction metrics (such as time-to-first-token stats) from an asynchronous stream?

docs.title: identifier
docs.text:
Yes, you can. When loading a model using the lms command-line interface, you can assign it a custom alias or identifier using the --identifier flag.

This is especially useful if you have an application or script expecting a specific model name (e.g., gpt-4 or a custom identifier like minimax) regardless of the underlying weights file you actually loaded.

docs.title: How to do it via CLI
docs.text:
Run the lms load command and pass your custom name into the --identifier flag:

lms load <your-model-key> --identifier "my-custom-name"

Example:

lms load openai/gpt-oss-120b --identifier "gpt-4o"

Once loaded this way, any API calls, client scripts, or tools querying your local LM Studio server can reference the model using "gpt-4o" as the model name parameter.

docs.title: 📚 CPU‑Only LLM Guide – Linux, macOS, Windows (Git Bash)
docs.text:
You can run a language model locally without a GPU on every major desktop OS. The guide is split into three “toolchains” – pick the one that matches your workflow:

Tool When it shines Typical RAM needed (4‑bit) How you start it Ollama One‑click CLI / REST, no Python needed 6‑7 GB for 7 B models, 1 GB for 1 B models ollama run … llama.cpp Ultra‑light binary you can embed anywhere 1‑6 GB depending on model size llama-cli … 🤗 Transformers + bitsandbytes Full Python control (fine‑tuning, pipelines) 0.5‑6 GB (depends on model) model.generate …

Rule of thumb: stay at ≤ 7 B parameters and use 4‑bit (q4_0 / nf4) quantisation – this fits in 8‑16 GB RAM and runs at a usable speed on a modern CPU.

Below are the exact commands for Linux, macOS, and Windows (Git Bash) for each tool. After the OS‑specific sections you’ll find a tiny Python demo that works on any platform (it uses the smallest model, DistilGPT‑2, so it fits even on a modest laptop).

docs.title: 1.1 Ollama
docs.text:
# Install (adds a systemd service)
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

# Pull a 4‑bit 7 B model (≈6 GB RAM)
ollama pull llama2:7b-q4_0

# Or a 1 B model (≈1 GB RAM) for quick testing
ollama pull tinyllama:1b-q4_0

Chat 

ollama run llama2:7b-q4_0   # interactive REPL

REST API (use from any language) 

curl -X POST http://localhost:11434/api/chat \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{
           "model":"llama2:7b-q4_0",
           "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain the difference between RAM and VRAM."}]
         }' | jq .

Performance tip – limit threads so your desktop stays responsive:

export OLLAMA_NUM_THREADS=4   # put in ~/.bashrc or run before starting Ollama
systemctl restart ollama.service   # reload if you changed the variable

docs.title: 1.2 llama.cpp
docs.text:
# Download the pre‑built binary
wget https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/releases/download/b1.7/llama.cpp-linux-x86_64.zip
unzip llama.cpp-linux-x86_64.zip
chmod +x llama-cli   # the executable is called `llama-cli`

docs.title: Convert a Hugging‑Face checkpoint (run once)
docs.text:
# Example: TinyLlama‑1.1B‑Chat (≈1 GB after q4_0)
git clone https://huggingface.co/TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v0.1
cd TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v0.1

# Convert to GGML 4‑bit (q4_0)
../llama-cli convert_hf_to_ggml.py --outtype q4_0 \
                                   --outfile ../tinyllama-q4_0.ggmlv3.bin .

docs.title: Run inference
docs.text:
../llama-cli -m tinyllama-q4_0.ggmlv3.bin \
             -p "Write a haiku about sunrise." \
             -n 48   # generate 48 tokens

You can call llama-cli from any script (subprocess.run([...])) or wrap it with FastAPI/Flask for a custom HTTP server.

docs.title: 1.3 Python 🤗 Transformers + bitsandbytes
docs.text:
# CPU‑only PyTorch (no CUDA)
pip install torch==2.4.0+cpu -f https://download.pytorch.org/whl/torch_stable.html

# Transformers + bitsandbytes for 4/8‑bit quantisation
pip install transformers bitsandbytes accelerate

docs.title: Load a 4‑bit 7 B model (Mistral‑7B‑Instruct)
docs.text:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch, bitsandbytes as bnb

model_name = "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2"

quant_cfg = bnb.nn.Int8Params(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.float16,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4"
)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_name,
    device_map="cpu",
    quantization_config=quant_cfg,
    trust_remote_code=True
)

def generate(prompt, max_new=80):
    inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt")
    out = model.generate(**inputs,
                         max_new_tokens=max_new,
                         temperature=0.8,
                         do_sample=True)
    return tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

print(generate("Summarise the plot of *The Little Prince* in three sentences."))

Thread‑limit (optional but useful) 

torch.set_num_threads(4)   # adjust to the number of cores you want to allocate

docs.title: 2️⃣ macOS
docs.text:
The commands are identical to the Linux ones; the only differences are:

  • Use brew to install git or wget if they are missing.
  • On Apple Silicon (M1/M2) the pre‑built llama.cpp binaries are also available – just pick the arm64 zip.
brew install wget   # if you don’t have it

Then follow the Linux steps for Ollama, llama.cpp, or Python. Ollama provides a .pkg installer for macOS as an alternative to the shell script:

curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh   # works on macOS too

docs.title: 3️⃣ Windows (using Git Bash)
docs.text:
Why Git Bash? It gives you a Unix‑like shell (bash) on Windows, so the same commands used on Linux/macOS work unchanged.

  1. Install Git Bash – download from https://git-scm.com/download/win and choose the default options (make sure “Git Bash Here” is enabled).

  2. Open “Git Bash” and run the same commands as in the Linux section.

docs.title: 3.1 Ollama on Windows
docs.text:
# In Git Bash
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh   # installs a Windows service
ollama pull llama2:7b-q4_0
ollama run llama2:7b-q4_0

The service runs in the background; you can still call the REST API from PowerShell, CMD, or any programming language.

docs.title: 3.2 llama.cpp on Windows
docs.text:
# Download the Windows zip (x86_64) – Git Bash can handle wget
wget https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/releases/download/b1.7/llama.cpp-windows-x86_64.zip
unzip llama.cpp-windows-x86_64.zip

cd TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v0.1
../llama-cli.exe convert_hf_to_ggml.py --outtype q4_0 \
                                       --outfile ../tinyllama-q4_0.ggmlv3.bin .

Run it:

../llama-cli.exe -m tinyllama-q4_0.ggmlv3.bin -p "Write a haiku about sunrise." -n 48

Then use the same Python snippet shown for Linux/macOS.

docs.title: Load a 4‑bit 7 B model (Mistral‑7B‑Instruct)
docs.text:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch, bitsandbytes as bnb

model_name = "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2"

quant_cfg = bnb.nn.Int8Params(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.float16,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4"
)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_name,
    device_map="cpu",
    quantization_config=quant_cfg,
    trust_remote_code=True
)

def generate(prompt, max_new=80):
    inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt")
    out = model.generate(**inputs,
                         max_new_tokens=max_new,
                         temperature=0.8,
                         do_sample=True)
    return tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

print(generate("Summarise the plot of *The Little Prince* in three sentences."))

Optional thread‑limit (helps keep the system responsive) 

torch.set_num_threads(4)   # adjust to how many cores you want to allocate

Pick the toolchain that matches your workflow:
